entry.sum: A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the behaviour of a dynamical system as a parameter passes a critical value: equilibria are created or destroyed, exchange stability, or give birth to periodic orbits. Near a bifurcation the system looks like one of a few simple normal forms, such as $\dot x = r + x^2$ (saddle-node), $\dot x = rx - x^2$ (transcritical), $\dot x = rx - x^3$ (pitchfork) and, in the plane, the Hopf bifurcation that creates a limit cycle.
key: \dot x = r + x^2:\ \text{two equilibria } x^* = \pm\sqrt{-r} \text{ for } r<0,\ \text{none for } r>0
f(x_0,r_0)=0,\ f_x(x_0,r_0)=0,\ f_{xx}\ne 0,\ f_r \ne 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{saddle-node at } (x_0,r_0)
\text{Hopf: } \dot r = \mu r - r^3,\ \dot\theta = \omega \;\Rightarrow\; \text{stable cycle of radius } \sqrt{\mu} \text{ for } \mu>0
entry.why: Bifurcations explain tipping points: a fishery that collapses when the harvest rate creeps past a threshold, a beam that buckles under a growing load, a laser that switches on, or a steady flow that starts to oscillate. They are also one route by which simple systems become chaotic, through cascades of period doublings.

links.note: Buckling of an elastic beam under compression is a pitchfork bifurcation, and the onset of oscillation in many physical and chemical systems is a Hopf bifurcation.
Near a bifurcation the restoring force vanishes, so noisy systems show 'critical slowing down': larger and longer-lasting fluctuations, used as an early-warning signal of tipping points.
Numerical continuation methods follow branches of equilibria as a parameter varies and detect folds and Hopf points along the way.

blocks.body:
Most equations that model the real world contain parameters: a growth rate, a load, a voltage, a harvesting quota. Usually a small change in a parameter makes a small change in behaviour: an equilibrium moves a little, a decay gets a little faster. But at certain special parameter values the picture changes in kind. Two equilibria collide and vanish; a stable state becomes unstable and hands its stability to a neighbour; a resting state starts to oscillate. These events are bifurcations.

This page assumes the language of [[phase-plane]]: equilibria, linearisation and stability. The pleasant surprise of the subject is that, although there are infinitely many possible systems, only a handful of bifurcations happen in a typical one-parameter family, and each is captured by a short polynomial model called a normal form.

blocks.title: One-dimensional flows and a first collision
blocks.body:
Start on the line: $\dot x = f(x, r)$, where $r$ is a parameter. Equilibria are the zeros $x^*$ of $f(\cdot, r)$, and an equilibrium is stable if $f_x(x^*, r) < 0$ (nearby points flow towards it) and unstable if $f_x(x^*, r) > 0$. When $f_x(x^*, r) \ne 0$ the equilibrium is called hyperbolic, and a small change in $r$ only moves it slightly without changing its stability. So bifurcations can only happen where $f = 0$ and $f_x = 0$ at the same time.

The simplest example is $\dot x = r + x^2$. Look at three values of $r$:

- $r = -1$: equilibria at $x = -1$ (stable, since $f_x = 2x = -2 < 0$) and $x = +1$ (unstable).
- $r = 0$: a single equilibrium at $x = 0$, stable from the left and unstable from the right (half-stable).
- $r = 1$: $\dot x = 1 + x^2 \ge 1$, so there is no equilibrium at all and every trajectory runs off to $+\infty$, in fact in finite time.

In general, for $r < 0$ there are two equilibria $\pm\sqrt{-r}$ which approach each other as $r$ increases, merge at $r = 0$ and disappear. This is a saddle-node bifurcation (also called a fold or a blue-sky bifurcation). Just after the bifurcation the flow is still slow near $x = 0$: trajectories need time about $\pi/\sqrt{r}$ to pass this 'ghost' of the vanished equilibria.

blocks.title: Bifurcation and bifurcation diagram
blocks.body: A family $\dot x = f(x, r)$ undergoes a bifurcation at $r = r_0$ if arbitrarily close to $r_0$ there are parameter values $r$ whose phase portrait is not topologically equivalent to the portrait at $r_0$ itself; topologically equivalent means that some homeomorphism (a continuous change of coordinates with continuous inverse) carries trajectories to trajectories, preserving the direction of time. Comparing with $r_0$ itself matters: in the transcritical example below, the portraits just below and just above $r_0$ are equivalent to each other (one repeller to the left of one attractor), but not to the single half-stable point at $r_0$. The bifurcation diagram plots the equilibria (and, in higher dimensions, other invariant sets such as periodic orbits) against the parameter, drawing stable branches solid and unstable branches dashed.

blocks.title: The three local bifurcations on the line
blocks.body:
Three normal forms cover what typically happens in one dimension.

1. Saddle-node, $\dot x = r + x^2$: a pair of equilibria, one stable and one unstable, is created or destroyed. The branches form a parabola $r = -x^2$ in the $(r, x)$ plane.

2. Transcritical, $\dot x = rx - x^2$: the equilibria $x = 0$ and $x = r$ exist for every $r$. Since $f_x = r - 2x$, the origin has $f_x = r$ and the other branch has $f_x = -r$. For $r < 0$ the origin is stable and $x = r$ unstable; for $r > 0$ they have swapped. Two branches cross and exchange stability. This is the natural bifurcation when one equilibrium is forced to exist for every parameter value, as with zero population or a laser that is off.

3. Pitchfork, $\dot x = rx - x^3$: the symmetry $x \mapsto -x$ forces equilibria to come in pairs. For $r \le 0$ only $x = 0$ exists and it is stable. For $r > 0$ the origin becomes unstable ($f_x = r > 0$) and two new stable equilibria $\pm\sqrt{r}$ appear. This is the supercritical pitchfork: the system smoothly chooses one of two symmetric states, like a vertical ruler that bows to the left or right when pressed from above.

The subcritical pitchfork $\dot x = rx + x^3$ is the dangerous version: for $r < 0$ the stable origin is flanked by two unstable equilibria $\pm\sqrt{-r}$, which shrink onto it as $r \to 0$. For $r > 0$ nothing nearby is stable and trajectories jump far away. In real systems higher-order terms usually stop the jump; for $\dot x = rx + x^3 - x^5$ the outer branches $x^2 = \tfrac12\left(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4r}\right)$ are stable and exist for $r > -\tfrac14$. Between $r = -\tfrac14$ and $r = 0$ both the origin and the outer branches are stable, so the state you observe depends on history. Increasing $r$ past 0 makes the system jump to the outer branch; decreasing it again, it stays there until $r = -\tfrac14$, where the outer branch dies in a saddle-node and the system drops back. This lag is hysteresis.

blocks.title: Saddle-node conditions
blocks.body:
Let $f(x, r)$ be twice continuously differentiable near $(x_0, r_0)$ with
$$f(x_0, r_0) = 0,\quad f_x(x_0, r_0) = 0,\quad f_{xx}(x_0, r_0) 
e 0,\quad f_r(x_0, r_0) 
e 0.$$
Then near $(x_0, r_0)$ the equilibria form a single curve $r = g(x)$ with $g(x_0) = r_0$, $g'(x_0) = 0$ and $g''(x_0) = -f_{xx}/f_r 
e 0$. On one side of $r_0$ there are exactly two equilibria close to $x_0$, of opposite stability; on the other side there are none.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Because $f_r(x_0, r_0) \ne 0$, the implicit function theorem (see [[inverse-function-theorem]]) says that near $(x_0, r_0)$ the zero set of $f$ is the graph of a unique $C^2$ function $r = g(x)$, so $f(x, g(x)) = 0$. Differentiating once gives $f_x + f_r\, g' = 0$, so $g'(x_0) = -f_x/f_r = 0$. Differentiating again,
$$f_{xx} + 2 f_{xr}\, g' + f_{rr}\, (g')^2 + f_r\, g'' = 0,$$
and at $x_0$, where $g' = 0$, this gives $g''(x_0) = -f_{xx}/f_r \ne 0$. So $g$ has a strict local maximum or minimum at $x_0$: each $r$ on one side of $r_0$ (close to it) is hit by exactly two values of $x$ near $x_0$, one on each side of $x_0$, and each $r$ on the other side is not hit at all.

For stability, $f_x(x, g(x)) = -f_r\, g'(x)$ along the curve. Since $g'' (x_0)\ne 0$, $g'$ changes sign at $x_0$, and $f_r$ keeps its sign near $(x_0,r_0)$. So the two equilibria have $f_x$ of opposite signs: one is stable and one unstable.

blocks.title: In the plane: the Hopf bifurcation
blocks.body:
In two or more dimensions an equilibrium can lose stability in a second way. Linearise at the equilibrium: stability is lost when an eigenvalue of the Jacobian crosses the imaginary axis. If a real eigenvalue passes through 0, we are back to the saddle-node, transcritical and pitchfork pictures along one direction. If instead a complex pair $\mu \pm i\omega$ with $\omega \ne 0$ crosses, the equilibrium changes from a stable spiral to an unstable spiral, and the typical outcome is a Hopf bifurcation: a small periodic orbit is born.

The model case is, in polar coordinates,
$$\dot r = \mu r - r^3,\qquad \dot\theta = \omega.$$
The radial equation is a pitchfork in $r \ge 0$. For $\mu < 0$ every trajectory spirals into the origin. For $\mu > 0$ the origin repels and the circle $r = \sqrt{\mu}$ attracts every other trajectory: it is a stable limit cycle (see [[limit-cycles]]), with radius $\sqrt{\mu}$ and period $2\pi/\omega$. This is a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. With $\dot r = \mu r + r^3$ it is subcritical: an unstable cycle shrinks onto the origin as $\mu \to 0^-$, and after the bifurcation trajectories leave the neighbourhood, with the same hysteresis story as before.

Whether a given Hopf bifurcation is super- or subcritical is decided by the quadratic and cubic terms of the system's Taylor expansion at the equilibrium (through the first Lyapunov coefficient). There are also global bifurcations, such as a cycle colliding with a saddle, and for maps the period-doubling bifurcation, where a multiplier passes through $-1$.

blocks.title: Reading off a saddle-node
blocks.body: Find and classify the bifurcation in $\dot x = r - \cosh x$, and give the equilibria at $r = 2$.
blocks.solution:
Equilibria satisfy $\cosh x = r$. Since $\cosh x \ge 1$ with equality only at $x = 0$, there are none for $r < 1$, one ($x = 0$) for $r = 1$, and two, $x = \pm\operatorname{arccosh} r = \pm \ln\left(r + \sqrt{r^2 - 1}\right)$, for $r > 1$.

Check the theorem's conditions at $(x_0, r_0) = (0, 1)$: $f = 0$; $f_x = -\sinh x = 0$; $f_{xx} = -\cosh 0 = -1 \ne 0$; $f_r = 1 \ne 0$. So this is a saddle-node, and $g''(0) = -f_{xx}/f_r = 1 > 0$: the curve of equilibria $r = \cosh x$ opens towards larger $r$, matching what we found.

Stability: $f_x = -\sinh x$ is negative for $x > 0$, so the right equilibrium is stable and the left one unstable. At $r = 2$ they are $x = \pm\ln(2 + \sqrt 3) \approx \pm 1.317$.

blocks.title: Harvesting a population
blocks.body: A fish population (in units of the carrying capacity) obeys $\dot x = x(1 - x) - h$, where $h \ge 0$ is a constant harvesting rate. Describe the equilibria as $h$ grows, and explain what happens if $h$ is raised slightly above the critical value.
blocks.solution:
Setting $x - x^2 = h$ gives $x_\pm = \tfrac12\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4h}\right)$, real exactly when $h \le \tfrac14$. Here $f_x = 1 - 2x$, which is negative at $x_+ > \tfrac12$ and positive at $x_- < \tfrac12$. So $x_+$ is the stable, healthy population and $x_-$ is an unstable threshold: a population pushed below $x_-$ (say by a bad year) collapses.

For example, $h = 0.21$ gives $\sqrt{1 - 0.84} = 0.4$, so $x_+ = 0.7$ and $x_- = 0.3$.

As $h \to \tfrac14$ the two equilibria merge at $x = \tfrac12$: a saddle-node. The maximum sustainable yield is $h = \tfrac14$, but it sits right on the bifurcation. For $h$ slightly above $\tfrac14$, $\dot x \le \tfrac14 - h < 0$ everywhere, so the population declines to zero however large it was, at first slowly (passing the ghost near $x = \tfrac12$) and then quickly. Lowering $h$ back below $\tfrac14$ after the crash does not help if $x$ has already fallen below $x_-$.

blocks.title: A Hopf bifurcation in Cartesian form
blocks.body: Show that $\dot x = \mu x - y - x(x^2 + y^2)$, $\dot y = x + \mu y - y(x^2 + y^2)$ undergoes a supercritical Hopf bifurcation at $\mu = 0$.
blocks.solution:
The Jacobian at the origin is $\begin{pmatrix} \mu & -1 \\ 1 & \mu \end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $\mu \pm i$. They cross the imaginary axis at $\mu = 0$ with nonzero speed ($\tfrac{d}{d\mu}\operatorname{Re} = 1$) and nonzero imaginary part, the setting for a Hopf bifurcation.

To see which kind, pass to polar coordinates, using $r\dot r = x\dot x + y\dot y$ and $r^2 \dot\theta = x\dot y - y\dot x$:
$$x\dot x + y\dot y = \mu(x^2 + y^2) - (x^2 + y^2)^2,\qquad x\dot y - y\dot x = x^2 + y^2.$$
So $\dot r = \mu r - r^3$ and $\dot\theta = 1$: exactly the normal form. For $\mu > 0$ there is a stable limit cycle $x^2 + y^2 = \mu$, traversed with period $2\pi$; for $\mu \le 0$ the origin attracts everything.

blocks.title: Period doubling in the logistic map
blocks.body: For the map $x_{n+1} = a x_n (1 - x_n)$ on $[0,1]$ with $1 < a \le 4$, find the nonzero fixed point and the value of $a$ where it loses stability, and show that a stable 2-cycle exists for $3 < a < 1 + \sqrt 6$.
blocks.solution:
For a map $x \mapsto F(x)$ a fixed point $p$ is stable when $|F'(p)| < 1$. The fixed points of $F(x) = ax(1-x)$ are $0$ and $p = 1 - 1/a$, and $F'(p) = a(1 - 2p) = 2 - a$. So $p$ is stable for $1 < a < 3$, and at $a = 3$ its multiplier passes through $-1$: a period-doubling bifurcation.

Points of period 2 solve $F(F(x)) = x$. This quartic has the fixed points $0$ and $p$ as roots; dividing them out leaves
$$a^2 x^2 - a(a+1)x + (a+1) = 0,\qquad x = \frac{(a+1) \pm \sqrt{(a+1)(a-3)}}{2a},$$
real and distinct exactly when $a > 3$. Call the roots $u, v$; then $F(u) = v$ and $F(v) = u$. The cycle is stable when $|(F\circ F)'(u)| = |F'(u)F'(v)| < 1$. Using $u + v = (a+1)/a$ and $uv = (a+1)/a^2$ from the quadratic,
$$F'(u)F'(v) = a^2(1 - 2u)(1 - 2v) = a^2\left(1 - 2(u+v) + 4uv\right) = -a^2 + 2a + 4.$$
This equals $1$ at $a = 3$ and $-1$ when $a^2 - 2a - 5 = 0$, that is $a = 1 + \sqrt 6 \approx 3.449$, and lies strictly between them in between. At $a = 1+\sqrt6$ the 2-cycle period-doubles into a 4-cycle, and so on: see [[chaos]].

blocks.body:
- $f_x = 0$ at an equilibrium is necessary for a bifurcation, not sufficient. In $\dot x = r - x^3$ the equilibrium $x = 0$ at $r = 0$ has $f_x = 0$, but for every $r$ there is exactly one equilibrium $x = r^{1/3}$, always stable: nothing qualitative changes. The theorem's condition $f_{xx} \ne 0$ fails here.
- Stability of an equilibrium is not the whole story near a subcritical bifurcation: a stable state can have a tiny basin of attraction, so small disturbances cause large jumps.
- For maps the stability test is $|F'(p)| < 1$, not $F'(p) < 0$.

Equilibria and their linearisations, the raw material of this page, come from [[phase-plane]]; for systems of equations the eigenvalue test is in [[ode-systems]] and [[eigen]]. The Hopf bifurcation is one of the main sources of the periodic orbits studied in [[limit-cycles]]. Repeated period doublings, as in the logistic map example, accumulate at a finite parameter value beyond which the motion is chaotic; that story, with Feigenbaum's universal ratio $4.669\ldots$, continues in [[chaos]]. The implicit function theorem behind the saddle-node proof is in [[inverse-function-theorem]], and continuation of branches of solutions is a standard tool in [[root-finding]].

1. Find and classify the bifurcation points of $\dot x = rx - \ln(1 + x)$ near $x = 0$, and of $\dot x = x(r - e^x)$.
2. Sketch the bifurcation diagram of $\dot x = r + x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}$ and find the two saddle-node values of $r$. Describe the hysteresis loop.
3. Show that $\dot x = r - x^2 - x^4$ has a saddle-node at $r = 0$ by checking the four conditions of the theorem.
4. For $\dot r = \mu r + r^3 - r^5$, $\dot\theta = 1$, find all limit cycles as a function of $\mu$ and say which are stable.

entry.sum: A limit cycle is an isolated closed orbit of a dynamical system: a periodic motion that nearby trajectories spiral towards (or away from). It models self-sustained oscillations whose amplitude is fixed by the system itself, not by the initial conditions. In the plane, the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem guarantees a closed orbit inside any bounded trapping region that contains no equilibria, which is also why planar flows can never be chaotic.
key: \dot r = r(1 - r^2),\ \dot\theta = 1:\quad r(t) \to 1 \text{ for every } r(0) > 0
\text{trajectory trapped in compact } R \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \text{ without equilibria} \;\Longrightarrow\; R \text{ contains a closed orbit}
\operatorname{div}(\varphi F) > 0 \text{ (or } < 0) \text{ throughout a simply connected region} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{no closed orbits there}
entry.why: Heartbeats, the firing of neurons, predator-prey cycles, chemical clocks and electronic oscillators all repeat with a characteristic amplitude and period that return after a disturbance; limit cycles are the mathematical form of that robustness. The theory also tells you when such oscillations are impossible, which is often just as useful.

links.note: Self-excited oscillators such as the Van der Pol circuit, bowed violin strings and clocks have limit cycles whose amplitude is set by a balance of energy input and dissipation.
The Poincaré–Bendixson theorem rests on the Jordan curve theorem, and the fact that a closed orbit must enclose an equilibrium is a case of index theory and the Brouwer fixed point theorem.
Periodic orbits are located numerically by shooting methods that find a fixed point of the Poincaré return map.

blocks.body:
Give a swing one push and it oscillates with an amplitude that depends on how hard you pushed, then dies away. A pendulum clock is different: start it with a small swing or a large one, and within minutes it settles to the same swing with the same period. The clock's escapement feeds in energy when the swing is small, friction removes it when the swing is large, and the balance picks out one particular oscillation.

In the phase plane (see [[phase-plane]]) the first kind of motion is a family of nested closed orbits around a centre, and the second is a single isolated closed orbit that attracts its neighbours: a limit cycle. This page explains how to recognise limit cycles, how to prove they exist without solving the equations, and how to prove that a system has none.

blocks.title: Limit cycle
blocks.body:
For a system $\dot{\mathbf x} = F(\mathbf x)$ in the plane, a closed orbit is the trajectory of a non-equilibrium solution with $\mathbf x(t + T) = \mathbf x(t)$ for some $T > 0$; the least such $T$ is the period. A limit cycle is a closed orbit $\Gamma$ that is isolated: some neighbourhood of $\Gamma$ contains no other closed orbit. It is stable (attracting) if all nearby trajectories approach $\Gamma$ as $t \to \infty$, unstable if they all approach it as $t \to -\infty$, and half-stable if they approach from one side and leave on the other.

The isolation requirement is what separates a limit cycle from the closed orbits around a linear centre, which come in continuous families and are each neutral.

blocks.title: A cycle you can see: polar coordinates
blocks.body:
The cleanest example is written in polar coordinates:
$$\dot r = r(1 - r^2),\qquad \dot\theta = 1.$$
The angle increases steadily, and the radius obeys a one-dimensional equation with equilibria $r = 0$ (unstable, since $\dot r > 0$ for small $r > 0$) and $r = 1$ (stable). So every trajectory except the origin winds onto the unit circle, from inside or outside: the unit circle is a stable limit cycle of period $2\pi$.

Here we can even solve exactly. The radial equation is separable, and with $r(0) = r_0 > 0$,
$$r(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + C e^{-2t}}},\qquad C = \frac{1}{r_0^2} - 1.$$
Starting at $r_0 = \tfrac12$ gives $C = 3$; the distance to the cycle shrinks roughly like $e^{-2t}$. That exponential rate is the cycle's Floquet exponent, the analogue for periodic orbits of an eigenvalue at an equilibrium.

In Cartesian coordinates the same system is $\dot x = x - y - x(x^2+y^2)$, $\dot y = x + y - y(x^2+y^2)$, which is not obviously oscillatory. Most systems cannot be decoupled this neatly, and that is why we need theorems.

blocks.title: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem
blocks.body: Let $F$ be a continuously differentiable vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing a closed bounded set $R$. Suppose $R$ contains no equilibrium of $\dot{\mathbf x} = F(\mathbf x)$, and that there is a trajectory that starts in $R$ and stays in $R$ for all $t \ge 0$. Then either that trajectory is a closed orbit, or it spirals towards a closed orbit as $t \to \infty$. In either case $R$ contains a closed orbit.

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body:
Let $\mathbf x(t)$ be the trapped trajectory. Its $\omega$-limit set $\omega$, the set of points $\mathbf p$ with $\mathbf x(t_k) \to \mathbf p$ along some sequence $t_k \to \infty$, is nonempty (by compactness of $R$, see [[compactness]]), closed, contained in $R$ and invariant under the flow. Take $\mathbf p \in \omega$; it is not an equilibrium, so near $\mathbf p$ we can draw a short segment $L$ transverse to the flow, crossed by every nearby trajectory in the same direction.

The key planar fact is that a single trajectory meets $L$ in a monotone sequence of points. Indeed, between two consecutive crossings the trajectory together with the piece of $L$ between them forms a closed curve, which by the Jordan curve theorem splits the plane into an inside and an outside; the flow crosses $L$ in only one direction, so the trajectory cannot get back to the other side, and later crossings move steadily along $L$. A monotone sequence has only one limit, so $\omega$ meets $L$ in just one point.

Because $\omega$ is closed and invariant, the whole trajectory of $\mathbf p$ lies in $\omega$, and so does that trajectory's own $\omega$-limit set. Pick a point $\mathbf q$ of the latter (it is not an equilibrium, as $R$ has none) and a transversal $L'$ through $\mathbf q$. The trajectory of $\mathbf p$ comes back arbitrarily close to $\mathbf q$, so it crosses $L'$ again and again; but every crossing is a point of $\omega$ on $L'$, and there is only one such point. So the trajectory of $\mathbf p$ passes through the same point twice: it is a closed orbit. Finally, the crossings of $\mathbf x(t)$ with a transversal converge monotonically to that point, which means $\mathbf x(t)$ spirals onto the closed orbit. The full details are in the references; the essential ingredients are compactness, transversals and the Jordan curve theorem, which fails on surfaces such as the torus and has no counterpart for curves in three dimensions.

blocks.title: Using the theorem: trapping regions
blocks.body:
In practice one builds an annulus-shaped trapping region: a closed region $R$ with a hole around the equilibrium, such that on the boundary of $R$ the vector field points into $R$ (or along the boundary). Then every trajectory starting in $R$ stays there, $R$ has no equilibria because the equilibrium is in the hole, and the theorem gives a closed orbit in $R$.

Two facts guide where to look. First, any closed orbit in the plane must enclose at least one equilibrium. (Sketch: the closed orbit bounds a disc which the flow maps into itself; for each $n$, the Brouwer fixed point theorem gives a point $\mathbf p_n$ fixed by the time-$1/n$ map of the flow, and a limit point of the $\mathbf p_n$ is fixed by the time-$t$ map for every $t$, so it is an equilibrium.) Second, the Hopf bifurcation of [[bifurcations]] is a common way for a small cycle to be born around an equilibrium that has just become an unstable spiral, which is exactly the situation where the inner boundary of an annulus is easy to draw.

blocks.title: Bendixson–Dulac criterion
blocks.body:
Let $F = (f, g)$ be continuously differentiable on a simply connected open region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, and let $\varphi$ be a continuously differentiable function on $D$. If
$$\operatorname{div}(\varphi F) = \frac{\partial (\varphi f)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (\varphi g)}{\partial y}$$
is strictly positive throughout $D$, or strictly negative throughout $D$, then $\dot x = f$, $\dot y = g$ has no closed orbit lying entirely in $D$. With $\varphi = 1$ this is Bendixson's criterion.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Suppose $\Gamma \subset D$ is a closed orbit, and let $A$ be the region it encloses; since $D$ is simply connected, $A \subseteq D$. By Green's theorem (see [[vector-calculus]]),
$$\iint_A \operatorname{div}(\varphi F)\, dA = \oint_\Gamma \left(\varphi f\, dy - \varphi g\, dx\right).$$
Parametrise $\Gamma$ by the solution itself: along it $dx = f\, dt$ and $dy = g\, dt$, so the integrand on the right is $\varphi (f g - g f)\, dt = 0$. The right side vanishes, while the left side is a double integral of a continuous function of one strict sign over a region of positive area, so it is nonzero. This contradiction shows no such $\Gamma$ exists.

blocks.title: An annulus trapping region
blocks.body: Show that $\dot x = x - y - x(x^2 + 2y^2)$, $\dot y = x + y - y(x^2 + 2y^2)$ has a closed orbit in the annulus $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \le r \le 1$. Then find it exactly.
blocks.solution:
Write $Q = x^2 + 2y^2$. Then
$$x\dot x + y\dot y = (x^2 + y^2)(1 - Q),\qquad x\dot y - y\dot x = x^2 + y^2,$$
so in polar coordinates $\dot r = r(1 - Q)$ and $\dot\theta = 1$. Because $\dot\theta = 1$, the origin is the only equilibrium.

Since $r^2 \le Q \le 2r^2$: if $r < \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ then $Q < 1$ and $\dot r > 0$; if $r > 1$ then $Q > 1$ and $\dot r < 0$. So for any $a < \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}$ and $b > 1$ the annulus $a \le r \le b$ is a trapping region without equilibria, and Poincaré–Bendixson gives a closed orbit in it. Shrinking $a$ and $b$ towards $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$ and $1$, every closed orbit lies in $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} \le r \le 1$ (at the point of a closed orbit farthest from the origin $\dot r = 0$, which forces $r \le 1$ there; at the nearest point, similarly, $r \ge \tfrac1{\sqrt2}$).

This one can be solved. With $\theta$ as the clock, $dr/d\theta = r(1 - r^2(1 + \sin^2\theta))$. Put $w = 1/r^2$: then
$$\frac{dw}{d\theta} = -2w + 2 + 2\sin^2\theta = -2w + 3 - \cos 2\theta,$$
a linear equation (see [[ode-first]]). Trying $w = \tfrac32 + A\cos 2\theta + B\sin 2\theta$ gives $A = B = -\tfrac14$. Every other solution differs from this one by a multiple of $e^{-2\theta}$, so there is exactly one periodic solution and it attracts all others: the unique, stable limit cycle is
$$r^2 = \frac{1}{\tfrac32 - \tfrac14(\cos 2\theta + \sin 2\theta)},$$
with $r$ ranging between about $0.734$ and $0.934$, inside the annulus as promised.

blocks.title: Ruling out cycles with Dulac
blocks.body: Two species compete: $\dot x = x(3 - x - 2y)$, $\dot y = y(2 - x - y)$ with $x, y \ge 0$. Show that populations never oscillate periodically.
blocks.solution:
The axes are invariant (if $x = 0$ then $\dot x = 0$), so a closed orbit with positive populations would lie in the open quadrant $D = \{x > 0, y > 0\}$, which is simply connected. Plain divergence is $3 - 2x - 2y + 2 - x - 2y$, which changes sign, so try $\varphi = 1/(xy)$:
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{3 - x - 2y}{y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{2 - x - y}{x}\right) = -\frac1y - \frac1x < 0 \text{ on } D.$$
By the Dulac criterion there is no closed orbit in $D$. Trajectories are bounded ($\dot x < 0$ once $x > 3$ and $\dot y < 0$ once $y > 2$). By the full Poincaré–Bendixson theory, the $\omega$-limit set of a bounded planar trajectory with finitely many equilibria is an equilibrium, a closed orbit, or a loop of equilibria joined by trajectories; the same Green's theorem argument rules out such loops too, so every trajectory with positive populations settles to an equilibrium. The same choice $\varphi = 1/(xy)$ works for every Lotka–Volterra model $\dot x = x(a - bx - cy)$, $\dot y = y(d - ex - fy)$ with self-limitation $b, f > 0$: it gives $\operatorname{div}(\varphi F) = -b/y - f/x$.

blocks.title: The Van der Pol oscillator
blocks.body:
The equation $\ddot x - \mu(1 - x^2)\dot x + x = 0$, with $\mu > 0$, came from radio circuits in the 1920s. The middle term is negative damping (energy input) when $|x| < 1$ and ordinary damping when $|x| > 1$, so small oscillations grow and large ones shrink. Liénard's theorem covers equations $\ddot x + f(x)\dot x + g(x) = 0$ with $f, g$ continuously differentiable, $f$ even, $g$ odd with $g(x) > 0$ for $x > 0$, and $F(x) = \int_0^x f$ having a single positive zero $a$, with $F < 0$ on $(0, a)$ and $F$ positive, nondecreasing and tending to infinity for $x > a$. It states that there is exactly one limit cycle and that it is stable. For Van der Pol, $F(x) = \mu\left(\tfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right)$, with positive zero $\sqrt3$.

For small $\mu$ we can predict the amplitude. With energy $E = \tfrac12(x^2 + \dot x^2)$ we get $\dot E = \mu(1 - x^2)\dot x^2$. On a nearly circular orbit $x \approx A\cos t$, the average of $\dot E$ over one period is
$$\frac{\mu}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} (1 - A^2\cos^2 t)A^2\sin^2 t\, dt = \mu\left(\frac{A^2}{2} - \frac{A^4}{8}\right),$$
which is zero for $A = 2$, positive for smaller $A$ and negative for larger. So the cycle has amplitude close to 2 and period close to $2\pi$. Numerically, for $\mu = 1$ the amplitude is about $2.009$ and the period about $6.663$. For large $\mu$ the motion becomes a relaxation oscillation: slow drifts punctuated by fast jumps, with period growing like $(3 - 2\ln 2)\mu$.

- A closed orbit is not automatically a limit cycle. The orbits of $\ddot x + x = 0$ or of the Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model are all closed, but they form continuous families, and none is isolated.
- The region in Poincaré–Bendixson must contain no equilibria. A disc around a spiral source does not qualify; you need an annulus that excludes it.
- The theorem is genuinely two-dimensional. On a torus, the flow $\dot\theta_1 = 1$, $\dot\theta_2 = \sqrt 2$ has no equilibria and no closed orbits. In three dimensions the Lorenz system has bounded trajectories that approach neither an equilibrium nor a cycle.
- Dulac's criterion needs a simply connected region. For $\dot r = r(1 - r^2)$, $\dot\theta = 1$ and $\varphi = 1/(x^2+y^2)$ one finds $\operatorname{div}(\varphi F) = -2$ on the whole punctured plane, yet the unit circle is a closed orbit: the punctured plane has a hole.
- Poincaré–Bendixson proves existence, not uniqueness or stability; those need extra arguments, as in the annulus example or Liénard's theorem.

Limit cycles are often born in Hopf bifurcations, and can also appear and disappear in pairs or by colliding with saddles; see [[bifurcations]]. Their stability is analysed with the Poincaré return map on a transversal, the same tool that, in three or more dimensions, reveals [[chaos]]: there the Poincaré–Bendixson restriction disappears and trajectories can wander forever on a strange attractor. The proof of the theorem uses [[compactness]] and the topology of the plane, and the enclosure fact comes from the Brouwer fixed point theorem, which belongs to [[homology]]. The famous open part of Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles a polynomial system of degree $n$ can have; even for $n = 2$ no bound is known.

1. Show that $\dot x = y$, $\dot y = -x - y + x^3 - y^3$ has no closed orbits in the plane. (Hint: compute the divergence.)
2. For $\dot r = r(1 - r^2)(4 - r^2)$, $\dot\theta = 1$, find all limit cycles and their stability.
3. Use a trapping annulus to prove that $\dot x = x - y - x^3$, $\dot y = x + y - y^3$ has a closed orbit. (Hint: show $\dot r > 0$ for $0 < r < 1$ and $\dot r < 0$ for $r > \sqrt2$, and that the origin is the only equilibrium.)
4. Check that $F(x) = \mu(x^3/3 - x)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Liénard's theorem as stated above.

entry.sum: A deterministic system is chaotic when its long-term behaviour is aperiodic and depends sensitively on initial conditions: nearby states separate exponentially fast, at a rate measured by a positive Lyapunov exponent, so prediction fails beyond a short horizon even though nothing is random. Chaos already appears in one-dimensional maps such as $x \mapsto 4x(1-x)$, and in flows from three dimensions up, where trajectories can settle onto a strange attractor such as the Lorenz attractor.
key: |\delta_n| \approx |\delta_0|\, e^{\lambda n},\qquad \lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \ln |f'(x_k)|
h(\theta) = \sin^2\!\left(\tfrac{\pi\theta}{2}\right):\quad 4h(1-h) = h\circ T,\ \ T = \text{tent map};\ \ \lambda = \ln 2
\dot x = \sigma(y - x),\ \ \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y,\ \ \dot z = xy - \beta z
entry.why: Chaos sets a hard limit on prediction: weather forecasts lose skill after a week or two, not because the equations are unknown but because errors in the initial state grow exponentially. The same ideas explain irregular heartbeats, mixing of fluids and the long-term instability of some planetary orbits, and they underlie the use of chaotic maps as pseudo-random generators.

links.note: Chaotic maps have invariant probability measures, such as the density $1/(\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)})$ for $4x(1-x)$, so long time averages along a single orbit behave like expectations; ergodic theory makes this precise.
The doubling map acts on binary expansions as a shift, so its periodic points are rationals with odd denominators and counting them uses Möbius inversion.
Sensitive dependence means floating-point simulations of chaotic systems diverge from the true orbit quickly; shadowing theorems explain when computed orbits are still faithful to some true orbit.

blocks.body:
In 1961 Edward Lorenz restarted a weather simulation from numbers printed to three decimal places instead of six. The new run tracked the old one for a while and then went its own way completely. The equations were deterministic and the computer made no mistakes; a difference in the fourth decimal place had simply grown until it was as large as the weather itself.

This page explains how a deterministic rule can behave so unpredictably, how to measure the effect, and why it needs a little room to happen. It builds on [[bifurcations]], where the logistic map started to double its period, and on [[limit-cycles]], whose Poincaré–Bendixson theorem shows that planar flows are never chaotic.

blocks.title: Sensitive dependence in numbers
blocks.body:
Iterate the logistic map $f(x) = 4x(1-x)$ from two starting points that differ by $10^{-10}$: $x_0 = 0.3$ and $y_0 = 0.3 + 10^{-10}$. Computing with enough digits to be sure of the result, the gap $|x_n - y_n|$ is about

- $2.0 \times 10^{-9}$ after 5 steps,
- $4.6 \times 10^{-8}$ after 10 steps,
- $5.4 \times 10^{-5}$ after 20 steps,
- $0.04$ after 30 steps,
- $0.54$ after 35 steps,

after which the two orbits are unrelated. On average the gap doubles at each step, and $2^{33} \approx 10^{10}$: an error in the tenth decimal place costs about 33 steps of predictability, and each extra digit of accuracy buys only about 3.3 more steps. This logarithmic return on accuracy is the practical meaning of chaos.

The doubling has a simple source. To first order, $y_{n+1} - x_{n+1} \approx f'(x_n)(y_n - x_n)$, so after $n$ steps the gap has been multiplied by $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} f'(x_k)$. Taking logarithms and averaging leads to the Lyapunov exponent.

blocks.title: Lyapunov exponent
blocks.body:
For a differentiable map $f$ of an interval and a starting point $x_0$ with orbit $x_k = f^k(x_0)$, the Lyapunov exponent is
$$\lambda(x_0) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \ln|f'(x_k)|,$$
when the limit exists. For a flow $\dot{\mathbf x} = F(\mathbf x)$, the largest Lyapunov exponent is the long-run exponential growth rate $\lim_{t\to\infty} \frac1t \ln \|\delta\mathbf x(t)\|$ of a generic small perturbation, which evolves by the linearised equation $\dot{\delta \mathbf x} = DF(\mathbf x(t))\,\delta\mathbf x$.

A positive exponent means nearby orbits separate like $e^{\lambda n}$; a negative one means they converge, as near a stable fixed point or cycle.

blocks.title: Chaos (Devaney)
The tent map is chaotic
blocks.body: The tent map $T(\theta) = 2\theta$ for $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac12$, $T(\theta) = 2 - 2\theta$ for $\tfrac12 \le \theta \le 1$, is chaotic on $[0,1]$ in Devaney's sense, with $\delta = \tfrac12$. The map $h(\theta) = \sin^2(\pi\theta/2)$ is a homeomorphism of $[0,1]$ with $f \circ h = h \circ T$ for $f(x) = 4x(1-x)$, so the logistic map at parameter 4 is chaotic as well.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Cut $[0,1]$ into the $2^n$ intervals $I_{n,k} = [k/2^n, (k+1)/2^n]$. By induction on $n$, $T^n$ maps each $I_{n,k}$ linearly onto $[0,1]$ with slope $\pm 2^n$: true for $n = 1$, and each $I_{n+1,k}$ is mapped by $T$ linearly onto some $I_{n,j}$.

Density of periodic points: the graph of $T^n$ over $I_{n,k}$ is a straight segment running from height 0 to height 1 (or the reverse), so it crosses the diagonal, giving a point with $T^n\theta = \theta$ in every $I_{n,k}$. Every open interval contains some $I_{n,k}$ once $n$ is large.

Transitivity: if $U$ is open, it contains some $I_{n,k}$, so $T^n(U) = [0,1]$, which meets every $V$.

Sensitivity: given $\theta$ and a neighbourhood $U$, pick $I_{n,k} \subseteq U$. Its image under $T^n$ is all of $[0,1]$, so it contains points $y_0, y_1$ with $T^n y_0 = 0$ and $T^n y_1 = 1$. One of these is at distance at least $\tfrac12$ from $T^n\theta$.

For the logistic map, $f(h(\theta)) = 4\sin^2(\tfrac{\pi\theta}2)\cos^2(\tfrac{\pi\theta}2) = \sin^2(\pi\theta)$, and $h(T\theta) = \sin^2(\pi\theta)$ in both halves (using $\sin^2(\pi - \pi\theta) = \sin^2(\pi\theta)$). Since $h$ is a continuous increasing bijection, it carries periodic points to periodic points and open sets to open sets, so properties 1 and 2 transfer; property 3 transfers because $h^{-1}$ is uniformly continuous on the compact interval $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: The route to chaos in the logistic family
blocks.body:
For the family $x \mapsto ax(1-x)$, the fixed point $1 - 1/a$ is stable up to $a = 3$, where it period-doubles; the 2-cycle is stable until $a = 1 + \sqrt 6 \approx 3.4495$, the 4-cycle until $a \approx 3.5441$, and so on (see [[bifurcations]]). The doubling parameters $a_1 = 3, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ crowd together geometrically: the gaps shrink by a factor tending to Feigenbaum's constant
$$\delta = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n - a_{n-1}}{a_{n+1} - a_n} = 4.6692\ldots,$$
and they accumulate at $a_\infty \approx 3.5699$. Already the first ratio $(a_2 - a_1)/(a_3 - a_2)$ is about $4.75$. Remarkably, the same $\delta$ appears for every smooth family of one-hump maps with a quadratic maximum and has been measured in fluid and electronic experiments: it is universal.

Beyond $a_\infty$ chaotic parameters are interleaved with periodic windows. The largest begins at $a = 1 + \sqrt 8 \approx 3.828$, where a 3-cycle appears. By Sharkovskii's theorem, a continuous map of an interval with a point of period 3 has points of every period, and Li and Yorke showed in 1975 that it also has an uncountable 'scrambled' set of orbits that neither settle down nor stay together: their paper's title, 'Period three implies chaos', gave the subject its name.

blocks.title: Flows: the Lorenz equations and strange attractors
blocks.body:
A planar flow cannot be chaotic: by Poincaré–Bendixson a bounded trajectory approaches an equilibrium, a closed orbit or a loop of these. Three dimensions give room for trajectories to wind around without ever closing or crossing. Lorenz's model of convection,
$$\dot x = \sigma(y - x),\qquad \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y,\qquad \dot z = xy - \beta z,$$
with his values $\sigma = 10$, $\beta = 8/3$, $\rho = 28$, is the standard example.

Two features combine. First, the flow is dissipative: the divergence is $-(\sigma + 1 + \beta) = -41/3$, a constant, so any blob of initial conditions shrinks in volume like $e^{-41t/3}$. All trajectories are eventually trapped in a bounded region and crowd onto a set of zero volume, the attractor. Second, on the attractor the motion stretches: the largest Lyapunov exponent is about $0.906$, so tiny errors grow by a factor $e$ roughly every $1.1$ time units. A set that is shrinking in volume while stretching in some directions must fold back on itself over and over, like kneading dough, and the result has fine layered structure with fractal dimension about $2.06$ (the Kaplan–Yorke estimate $2 + \lambda_1/|\lambda_3|$, where $\lambda_3 = -\tfrac{41}{3} - \lambda_1$ because the exponents sum to the divergence and the middle one is 0).

An attractor with this combination of attraction and sensitive dependence is called a strange attractor. That the Lorenz equations really have one was proved only in 2002, by Warwick Tucker, with a computer-assisted proof. Maps give simpler examples: the Hénon map $(x, y) \mapsto (1 - ax^2 + y,\ bx)$ with $a = 1.4$, $b = 0.3$ has Jacobian determinant $-b$, so it shrinks areas by the factor $0.3$ at every step while stretching along the attractor.

blocks.title: Counting periodic orbits
blocks.body: How many points have least period exactly 6 under the tent map $T$ (equivalently under $4x(1-x)$), and how many distinct 6-cycles are there?
blocks.solution:
From the proof above, $T^n$ has exactly one fixed point in each of the $2^n$ intervals $I_{n,k}$ (its graph there is a single segment of slope $\pm 2^n$). Points found in different intervals are distinct, because a shared endpoint $k/2^n$ with $0 < k < 2^n$ is sent by $T^n$ to 0 or 1 and so is not fixed. Hence $T^n$ has exactly $2^n$ fixed points. (For the logistic map, $f^n(x) = x$ is a polynomial equation of degree $2^n$, and all $2^n$ roots are real and lie in $[0,1]$.)

A fixed point of $T^n$ has least period some divisor $d$ of $n$. Writing $N(d)$ for the number of points of least period $d$, we get $\sum_{d \mid n} N(d) = 2^n$, and [[mobius]] inversion gives
$$N(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, 2^{n/d}.$$
For $n = 6$: $N(6) = 2^6 - 2^3 - 2^2 + 2^1 = 64 - 8 - 4 + 2 = 54$. Each 6-cycle contains 6 points, so there are $54/6 = 9$ distinct 6-cycles. The same count for $n = 3$ gives $8 - 2 = 6$ points, that is, two 3-cycles.

blocks.title: The Lyapunov exponent of the logistic map at 4
blocks.body: Show that for almost every starting point, the Lyapunov exponent of $f(x) = 4x(1-x)$ equals $\ln 2$.
blocks.solution:
For the tent map $|T'| = 2$ everywhere except at $\tfrac12$, so every orbit that avoids $\tfrac12$ has exponent exactly $\ln 2$. Now transfer through the conjugacy: $f^n = h \circ T^n \circ h^{-1}$, so by the chain rule
$$(f^n)'(x) = h'(T^n\theta)\cdot (T^n)'(\theta) \cdot (h^{-1})'(x),\qquad \theta = h^{-1}(x).$$
The middle factor has absolute value $2^n$. The outer factors do not grow exponentially as long as the orbit does not hug the endpoints, where $h'$ vanishes; for a typical orbit they contribute $o(n)$ to the logarithm. Hence $\frac1n \ln |(f^n)'(x)| \to \ln 2$.

There is also a direct check. The uniform distribution on $[0,1]$ is invariant under $T$ (every interval has two preimages, each of half its length), and $h$ carries it to the density $\rho(x) = \dfrac{1}{\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)}}$. By the ergodic theorem the time average equals the space average:
$$\lambda = \int_0^1 \frac{\ln|4 - 8x|}{\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)}}\, dx = \ln 2,$$
which can be confirmed numerically.

blocks.title: Equilibria of the Lorenz system
blocks.body: Find the equilibria of the Lorenz equations for $\rho > 1$ and check that at $\rho = 28$ (with $\sigma = 10$, $\beta = 8/3$) all of them are unstable.
blocks.solution:
$\dot x = 0$ forces $y = x$; then $\dot z = 0$ gives $z = x^2/\beta$, and $\dot y = 0$ gives $x(\rho - 1 - z) = 0$. So either $x = y = z = 0$, or $z = \rho - 1$ and $x = y = \pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho - 1)}$. At $\rho = 28$ the two non-trivial equilibria are $C_\pm = (\pm 6\sqrt2, \pm 6\sqrt2, 27)$, about $(\pm 8.49, \pm 8.49, 27)$.

At the origin the Jacobian has the eigenvalue $-\beta$ and the eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix} -\sigma & \sigma \\ \rho & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant $\sigma(1 - \rho) < 0$ forces one positive eigenvalue: a saddle. At $C_\pm$ the eigenvalues are approximately $-13.85$ and $0.094 \pm 10.19i$; the positive real part makes them unstable spirals. (They lose stability in a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at $\rho = \sigma(\sigma + \beta + 3)/(\sigma - \beta - 1) = 470/19 \approx 24.74$.) With every equilibrium unstable and every trajectory trapped in a bounded region, a typical trajectory can never come to rest; numerically it never settles onto a cycle either, and instead wanders on the attractor.

blocks.body:
- Chaos is not randomness. The rule is deterministic, and over short times prediction works well; what fails is long-term prediction from imperfect data.
- Exponential separation alone is not chaos. The map $x \mapsto 2x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ separates points exponentially, but orbits just run off to infinity. Chaos needs stretching together with folding inside a bounded region.
- A positive exponent estimated from a short simulation may be a transient: some systems behave chaotically for a long time before settling onto a stable cycle (transient chaos).
- Computed orbits of chaotic systems are not the true orbits from the given starting point: rounding errors are amplified like any other error. Statistical properties and attractor shapes are still reliable, and shadowing theorems explain why in many cases.
- 'Strange attractor' and 'chaotic attractor' are not quite synonyms: 'strange' refers to fractal geometry, 'chaotic' to sensitive dependence. The Lorenz attractor is both.

Chaos is where the two previous pages lead: period-doubling cascades from [[bifurcations]] and the escape from the planar restrictions of [[limit-cycles]]. The doubling map acts on binary expansions by shifting digits (see [[digits-bases]]), which is the simplest example of symbolic dynamics, and its periodic points were counted with [[mobius]] inversion. Long-run statistics of chaotic systems are the subject of ergodic theory, which links to [[probability-basics]] and to Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy, a dynamical cousin of [[entropy]]. Simulating chaotic flows reliably is a problem in [[numerical-odes]], and the Lorenz system came from a truncated model of fluid convection, a distant relative of [[navier-stokes]].

1. Show that the doubling map $D(\theta) = 2\theta \bmod 1$ has exactly $2^n - 1$ points with $D^n\theta = \theta$ in $[0, 1)$, and describe them in binary.
2. Compute the number of 4-cycles and 5-cycles of the tent map.
3. Show that every volume element of phase space shrinks under the Lorenz flow for any positive $\sigma$ and $\beta$, and find the rate.
4. For the map $x \mapsto 2x \bmod 1$, two points agree in their first 40 binary digits. Roughly how many iterations until they are on opposite halves of the interval?

entry.sum: A Fourier series writes a $2\pi$-periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines, $f(x) \sim \tfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n\ge1} (a_n \cos nx + b_n \sin nx)$, with each coefficient found by integrating against the matching wave. Orthogonality of the waves is what makes the coefficients easy to compute; for piecewise smooth functions the series converges to $f$, and to the midpoint of the jump at a discontinuity.
key: a_n = \frac1\pi \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx,\qquad b_n = \frac1\pi \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx
\frac1\pi \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)^2\,dx = \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n^2 + b_n^2\right)
x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx \ \ (|x|\le\pi) \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}
entry.why: Fourier introduced these series to solve the heat equation, and they remain the standard way to solve linear PDEs on intervals, to analyse sound and vibrations by frequency, and to compress signals. They also give slick evaluations of sums such as $\sum 1/n^2$ and $\sum 1/n^4$.

links.note: Separation of variables turns the heat, wave and Laplace equations on an interval into Fourier series whose coefficients come from the initial or boundary data.
A musical tone is a sum of harmonics with frequencies $n f_0$; the Fourier coefficients are the amplitudes of the overtones that give an instrument its timbre.
Parseval's identity applied to polynomials gives the values $\zeta(2k)$, and Fourier expansion on $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ underlies exponential sums and the circle method.

Körner, Fourier Analysis
Tolstov, Fourier Series

blocks.body:
A violin and a flute playing the same note produce air-pressure waves with the same period but different shapes. Fourier's discovery, made while studying how heat spreads, is that any reasonable periodic shape is a sum of pure sine and cosine waves with frequencies $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ times the basic one. The shape is then described by a list of numbers: how much of each frequency it contains.

This page shows how to find those numbers using the [[riemann-integral]], when the resulting infinite [[series]] really adds up to the function, and what goes wrong at jumps. The trigonometric facts needed are in [[trig]].

blocks.title: Orthogonality: the trick that finds coefficients
blocks.body:
Suppose a $2\pi$-periodic function can be written as
$$f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n\cos nx + b_n \sin nx\right).$$
How do we recover, say, $a_3$? Multiply both sides by $\cos 3x$ and integrate over $[-\pi, \pi]$. Using product-to-sum formulas one checks that for integers $m, n \ge 0$,
$$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos mx\cos nx\,dx = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin mx\sin nx\,dx = 0 \ (m \ne n),\qquad \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin mx\cos nx\,dx = 0,$$
while $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2 nx\,dx = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin^2 nx\,dx = \pi$ for $n \ge 1$. So every term dies except the $\cos 3x$ term, which gives $\pi a_3$. This is the same idea as finding the components of a vector by taking dot products with an orthogonal basis; here the dot product of two functions is $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f g$.

The factor $\tfrac12$ on $a_0$ is there so that a single formula covers $n = 0$ too. Since $e^{inx} = \cos nx + i\sin nx$, the series can also be written $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} c_n e^{inx}$ with $c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx$; for real $f$, $c_{\pm n} = \tfrac12(a_n \mp i b_n)$. The complex form is usually tidier in proofs.

blocks.title: Fourier coefficients and Fourier series
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be $2\pi$-periodic and Riemann integrable on $[-\pi,\pi]$. Its Fourier coefficients are
$$a_n = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx\ (n \ge 0),\qquad b_n = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx\ (n\ge1),$$
and its Fourier series is $\tfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n\ge1}(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)$. The $N$-th partial sum is written $S_N f(x)$. We write $f \sim$ (series) because, a priori, the series need not converge, nor converge to $f$.

For a function of period $2L$, replace $nx$ by $n\pi x/L$ and $\tfrac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi$ by $\tfrac1L\int_{-L}^L$.

blocks.title: First examples and a symmetry shortcut
blocks.body:
If $f$ is even, every $b_n = 0$ (the integrand $f\sin nx$ is odd); if $f$ is odd, every $a_n = 0$. That halves the work.

Take the square wave $f(x) = 1$ for $0 < x < \pi$, $f(x) = -1$ for $-\pi < x < 0$, extended periodically. It is odd, and
$$b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi \sin nx\,dx = \frac{2(1 - (-1)^n)}{\pi n},$$
which is $\frac{4}{\pi n}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$. So
$$f(x) \sim \frac4\pi\left(\sin x + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} + \frac{\sin 5x}{5} + \cdots\right).$$
At $x = \pi/2$, where $f = 1$ and $\sin(n\pi/2)$ runs through $1, 0, -1, 0, \ldots$, this predicts $1 = \frac4\pi(1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \cdots)$, Leibniz's series for $\pi/4$. At $x = 0$ every term is 0, which is the average of the left and right limits $-1$ and $1$. Both are instances of the theorem below.

The sawtooth $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ is odd, and integration by parts gives $b_n = \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$, so $x \sim 2\left(\sin x - \frac{\sin 2x}{2} + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} - \cdots\right)$. The coefficients decay only like $1/n$, reflecting the jump of the periodic extension at $x = \pm\pi$. Compare $x^2$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, whose periodic extension is continuous with a corner: its coefficients decay like $1/n^2$. In general, the smoother the periodic function, the faster its coefficients decay: if $f$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable and periodic, $k$ integrations by parts show $|a_n|, |b_n| \le C/n^k$.

blocks.title: Dirichlet's theorem (pointwise convergence)
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be $2\pi$-periodic and piecewise continuously differentiable: there are finitely many points in $[-\pi,\pi]$ (jumps or corners) away from which $f$ is continuously differentiable, and at each of them the one-sided limits $f(x^\pm)$ and the one-sided derivatives $\lim_{u\to0^+}\frac{f(x+u)-f(x^+)}{u}$ and $\lim_{u\to0^-}\frac{f(x+u)-f(x^-)}{u}$ exist. Then for every $x$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} S_Nf(x) = \frac{f(x^+) + f(x^-)}{2}.$$
In particular $S_N f(x) \to f(x)$ wherever $f$ is continuous.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Substituting the coefficient formulas into the partial sum and using $\cos n(x - t) = \cos nx \cos nt + \sin nx\sin nt$,
$$S_Nf(x) = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)\Big(\tfrac12 + \sum_{n=1}^N \cos n(x-t)\Big)dt = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x+u)\,D_N(u)\,du,$$
after substituting $t = x + u$ and using periodicity. Here $D_N(u) = \tfrac12 + \sum_{n=1}^N\cos nu$ is the Dirichlet kernel; multiplying by $2\sin(u/2)$ and telescoping $2\sin\frac u2\cos nu = \sin(n+\tfrac12)u - \sin(n-\tfrac12)u$ gives
$$D_N(u) = \frac{\sin\left((N+\tfrac12)u\right)}{2\sin(u/2)}.$$
$D_N$ is even and $\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi D_N = \tfrac12$ (integrate the cosine sum term by term). Hence
$$S_Nf(x) - \frac{f(x^+)+f(x^-)}2 = \frac1\pi\int_0^\pi g_+(u)\sin\left((N+\tfrac12)u\right)du + \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^0 g_-(u)\sin\left((N+\tfrac12)u\right)du,$$
with $g_+(u) = \dfrac{f(x+u) - f(x^+)}{2\sin(u/2)}$ on $(0,\pi]$ and $g_-$ defined similarly with $f(x^-)$ on $[-\pi,0)$. As $u \to 0^+$, $g_+(u) = \frac{f(x+u)-f(x^+)}{u}\cdot\frac{u}{2\sin(u/2)}$ tends to the one-sided derivative, so $g_+$ is bounded and piecewise continuous, hence integrable; likewise $g_-$.

It remains to show $\int_a^b g(u)\sin(\lambda u)\,du \to 0$ as $\lambda\to\infty$ for any integrable $g$ (the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma). If $g$ is a step function with $k$ steps, each piece contributes at most $\left|\int_\alpha^\beta \sin\lambda u\,du\right| \le 2/\lambda$ times the step height, so the integral tends to 0. A Riemann integrable $g$ can be approximated by a step function $s$ with $\int_a^b|g - s| < \varepsilon$, and then $\left|\int g\sin\lambda u\right| \le \varepsilon + \left|\int s\sin\lambda u\right|$, which is less than $2\varepsilon$ for large $\lambda$.

blocks.title: Energy: Bessel and Parseval
blocks.body:
Pythagoras for functions: since the waves are orthogonal, the 'energy' $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi f^2$ splits over frequencies. Expanding $0 \le \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (f - S_Nf)^2$ and using orthogonality gives Bessel's inequality,
$$\frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^N(a_n^2 + b_n^2) \le \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f^2,$$
so the squares of the coefficients always have a convergent sum, and in particular $a_n, b_n \to 0$. In fact equality holds in the limit: this is Parseval's identity, stated in the key statements above, valid for every Riemann integrable $f$. Equivalently, $\int_{-\pi}^\pi (f - S_Nf)^2 \to 0$: the partial sums converge to $f$ in mean square even when they fail to converge at some points. The proof needs one more ingredient, that trigonometric polynomials can approximate $f$ in mean square. Fejér's theorem supplies it: the averages $\sigma_N = \frac{1}{N+1}(S_0f + \cdots + S_Nf)$ converge uniformly to any continuous periodic $f$.

The geometric picture is that $\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx\}$ is a complete orthogonal system, an orthogonal basis of the space of square-integrable functions, which is a [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]].

blocks.title: The Basel sum from a parabola
blocks.body: Find the Fourier series of $f(x) = x^2$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and use it to evaluate $\sum_{n\ge1} 1/n^2$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}/n^2$.
blocks.solution:
$f$ is even, so $b_n = 0$, and $a_0 = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi x^2\,dx = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$. For $n \ge 1$, two integrations by parts give
$$a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos nx\,dx = \frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}.$$
The periodic extension is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable (with corners at odd multiples of $\pi$), so by Dirichlet's theorem
$$x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx\qquad (|x| \le \pi).$$
At $x = \pi$, $\cos n\pi = (-1)^n$, so $\pi^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum \frac1{n^2}$, giving $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$. At $x = 0$, $0 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} - 4\sum\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$, giving $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{12}$. (This is the value $\zeta(2)$ of the [[zeta]] function.)

blocks.title: Parseval and the sum of 1/n^4
blocks.body: Use Parseval's identity for $x^2$ to evaluate $\sum_{n\ge1} 1/n^4$.
blocks.solution:
The left side of Parseval is $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^4\,dx = \frac{2\pi^4}{5}$. On the right, $\frac{a_0^2}{2} = \frac12\left(\frac{2\pi^2}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{2\pi^4}{9}$ and $a_n^2 = \frac{16}{n^4}$. So
$$\frac{2\pi^4}{5} = \frac{2\pi^4}{9} + 16\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^4},\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^4} = \frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{8\pi^4}{45} = \frac{\pi^4}{90}.$$
The same identity for $f(x) = x$, where $b_n^2 = 4/n^2$ and $\frac1\pi\int x^2 = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$, gives $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$ again. Repeating with higher powers of $x$ produces $\zeta(2k)$ as a rational multiple of $\pi^{2k}$ for every $k$.

blocks.title: The Gibbs overshoot
blocks.body: For the square wave, the partial sums $S_N$ converge to $1$ at each fixed $x \in (0,\pi)$. Show that nevertheless $\max_{0 \lt x \lt \pi} S_N(x)$ does not tend to 1.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate the partial sum $S_{2M-1}(x) = \frac4\pi\sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{\sin(2k-1)x}{2k-1}$:
$$S_{2M-1}'(x) = \frac4\pi\sum_{k=1}^M\cos(2k-1)x = \frac{2\sin 2Mx}{\pi\sin x},$$
using the same telescoping trick as for $D_N$. The first critical point to the right of 0 is $x_M = \frac{\pi}{2M}$, and there
$$S_{2M-1}(x_M) = \frac4\pi\sum_{k=1}^M \frac{\sin\left((2k-1)\frac{\pi}{2M}\right)}{2k-1} = \frac2\pi\sum_{k=1}^M \frac{\sin t_k}{t_k}\cdot\frac{\pi}{M},\qquad t_k = \frac{(2k-1)\pi}{2M}.$$
This is a midpoint Riemann sum for $\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt \approx 1.1790$. So the partial sums overshoot the value 1 by about $0.179$, roughly $9\%$ of the jump from $-1$ to $1$, in a spike that narrows towards the jump but never shrinks in height. This is the Gibbs phenomenon: convergence at a jump is pointwise but not uniform.

blocks.body:
- A Fourier series need not converge to $f$ at a jump: it converges to the midpoint. It also matters where the periodic extension jumps: $x$ on $(-\pi,\pi)$ extends with jumps at $\pm\pi$, so its series gives 0 there, not $\pm\pi$.
- Continuity alone does not guarantee pointwise convergence. Du Bois-Reymond constructed a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point; some smoothness (as in Dirichlet's theorem) or a different summation method (Fejér) is needed.
- Term-by-term differentiation can fail. Differentiating the sawtooth series gives $2(\cos x - \cos 2x + \cdots)$, which diverges everywhere, because the periodic extension of $x$ is not continuous. Term-by-term integration, by contrast, is always safe for integrable $f$.
- Watch the normalisation: some books use $[0, 2\pi]$, period $2L$, or $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ in front, and the formulas change accordingly.

Separation of variables turns the [[heat-equation]], [[wave-equation]] and [[laplace-equation]] on bounded domains into Fourier series problems, and [[sturm-liouville]] theory generalises sines and cosines to the eigenfunctions of other differential operators. Letting the period tend to infinity turns sums into integrals and gives the [[fourier-transform]]. The mean-square theory is the prototype of orthogonal expansions in [[hilbert-spaces]] and [[lp-spaces]], and relations between a function's values and its Fourier coefficients, such as Poisson summation in [[fourier-poisson]], are central in analytic number theory.

1. Find the Fourier series of $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and deduce $\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{8}$.
2. Expand $f(x) = 1$ on $(0, \pi)$ as a sine series (the odd extension) and compare with the square wave.
3. Show that $\int_{-\pi}^\pi |D_N(u)|\,du \to \infty$ as $N \to \infty$ (compare $|D_N(u)|$ with $|\sin((N+\tfrac12)u)|/|u|$), and explain why this allows $|S_Nf(0)|$ to be large for some $f$ with $|f| \le 1$.
4. Use Parseval for the square wave to evaluate $\sum_{k\ge0}\frac1{(2k+1)^2}$ a second way.

entry.sum: The Fourier transform $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$ is the continuous analogue of Fourier series for functions on the whole line: it measures how much of each frequency $\xi$ a function contains, and $f$ is recovered by the inverse transform. It turns differentiation into multiplication by $2\pi i\xi$ and convolution into multiplication, which is why it solves linear constant-coefficient equations, and it preserves energy (Plancherel).
key: \hat f(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx,\qquad f(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat f(\xi)\,e^{2\pi i x\xi}\,d\xi
\widehat{f'}(\xi) = 2\pi i\xi\,\hat f(\xi),\qquad \widehat{f * g} = \hat f\,\hat g,\qquad \widehat{e^{-\pi x^2}} = e^{-\pi\xi^2}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(x)|^2\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |\hat f(\xi)|^2\,d\xi
entry.why: It is the basic tool for solving the heat, wave and Schrödinger equations on unbounded domains, for designing filters and analysing signals (through its discrete version, computed by the fast Fourier transform), and for proving the central limit theorem via characteristic functions. The uncertainty principle of quantum mechanics is a theorem about it.

links.note: The characteristic function of a random variable is the Fourier transform of its distribution; sums of independent variables correspond to products, which gives the cleanest proof of the central limit theorem.
The discrete Fourier transform approximates $\hat f$ from samples, and the fast Fourier transform computes it in $O(n\log n)$ operations, which makes spectral methods and fast convolution practical.
The quantum Fourier transform, a discrete Fourier transform on the amplitudes of a quantum register, is the key step in Shor's factoring algorithm.

blocks.body:
A [[fourier-series]] breaks a periodic function into waves whose frequencies are whole multiples of one basic frequency. Most signals are not periodic: a single clap, a pulse of light, a bump of heat in a long rod. The Fourier transform handles these by allowing every real frequency, with a continuous 'spectrum' $\hat f(\xi)$ in place of a list of coefficients.

The payoff is a dictionary in which calculus becomes algebra: derivatives become multiplications, convolutions become products, and many differential equations become equations you can solve by division. The definition uses [[improper-integrals]] over the whole line.

blocks.title: From series to integrals
blocks.body:
Take a function $f$ that vanishes outside some interval, and view it as one period of a function of large period $L$. Its complex Fourier series, with frequencies $n/L$ cycles per unit length, is
$$f(x) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} c_n e^{2\pi i nx/L},\qquad c_n = \frac1L\int_{-L/2}^{L/2} f(x)e^{-2\pi i nx/L}\,dx.$$
Define $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$. Then $c_n = \frac1L\hat f(n/L)$, and the series reads
$$f(x) = \sum_{n} \hat f\!\left(\tfrac nL\right)e^{2\pi i (n/L)x}\cdot\frac1L.$$
This is a Riemann sum with step $1/L$ for $\int \hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\xi}\,d\xi$. As $L\to\infty$ the allowed frequencies $n/L$ fill the line, and the sum becomes the inversion formula in the key statements. Conventions differ between books (some use $e^{-ix\xi}$ with factors $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ or $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$); the $2\pi$ in the exponent, used here, makes the formulas most symmetric.

blocks.title: Fourier transform
blocks.body:
Let $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb C$ be absolutely integrable, $\int_{-\infty}^\infty |f| < \infty$. Its Fourier transform is the function
$$\hat f(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R.$$
Since $|e^{-2\pi i x\xi}| = 1$, the integral converges absolutely, $|\hat f(\xi)| \le \int|f|$, and $\hat f$ is continuous. The variable $\xi$ is frequency, in cycles per unit of $x$.

blocks.title: Three transforms to know
blocks.body:
1. The box $\chi(x) = 1$ for $|x| \le \tfrac12$ and $0$ otherwise:
$$\hat\chi(\xi) = \int_{-1/2}^{1/2} e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx = \frac{\sin\pi\xi}{\pi\xi}\quad(\xi\ne0),\qquad \hat\chi(0) = 1.$$
This 'sinc' function decays only like $1/|\xi|$: the sharp edges of the box need high frequencies.

2. The two-sided exponential $e^{-|x|}$: splitting the integral at 0,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-|x|}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx = \frac{1}{1 + 2\pi i\xi} + \frac{1}{1 - 2\pi i\xi} = \frac{2}{1 + 4\pi^2\xi^2}.$$
A corner at $x = 0$ gives decay like $1/\xi^2$.

3. The Gaussian $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own transform (theorem below). Smooth and rapidly decaying, it has a smooth and rapidly decaying spectrum.

The pattern is general: smoothness of $f$ corresponds to decay of $\hat f$, and decay of $f$ to smoothness of $\hat f$. Two more rules are worth memorising. Shifting $f(x - a)$ multiplies the transform by $e^{-2\pi i a\xi}$. Stretching $f(x/a)$ with $a > 0$ gives $a\hat f(a\xi)$: wider in space means narrower in frequency.

blocks.title: The Gaussian is its own transform
blocks.body: For $g(x) = e^{-\pi x^2}$, $\hat g(\xi) = e^{-\pi\xi^2}$. More generally, for $a > 0$ the transform of $e^{-\pi a x^2}$ is $a^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/a}$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Set $F(\xi) = \hat g(\xi) = \int e^{-\pi x^2}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx$. Differentiating under the integral sign (justified because $x e^{-\pi x^2}$ is integrable),
$$F'(\xi) = \int e^{-\pi x^2}(-2\pi i x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx = i\int \left(e^{-\pi x^2}\right)'e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx.$$
Integrate by parts; the boundary terms vanish, and the derivative of $e^{-2\pi i x\xi}$ is $-2\pi i\xi e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$, so
$$F'(\xi) = -i\int e^{-\pi x^2}(-2\pi i\xi)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx = -2\pi\xi F(\xi).$$
The solutions of $F' = -2\pi\xi F$ are $F(\xi) = F(0)e^{-\pi\xi^2}$, and $F(0) = \int e^{-\pi x^2}\,dx = 1$. The general case follows from the stretching rule with $x \mapsto \sqrt a\,x$.

blocks.title: The dictionary
Convolution theorem
blocks.body: If $f$ and $g$ are absolutely integrable, then $f * g$ is absolutely integrable and $\widehat{f*g}(\xi) = \hat f(\xi)\,\hat g(\xi)$ for all $\xi$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Since $\iint |f(y)||g(x-y)|\,dy\,dx = \int|f|\cdot\int|g| < \infty$, Fubini's theorem lets us swap the order of integration (see [[multiple-integrals]]). Then
$$\widehat{f*g}(\xi) = \int\!\!\int f(y)g(x - y)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx\,dy = \int f(y)e^{-2\pi iy\xi}\left(\int g(x-y)e^{-2\pi i(x-y)\xi}\,dx\right)dy.$$
The inner integral is $\hat g(\xi)$ after substituting $t = x - y$, and what remains is $\hat f(\xi)\hat g(\xi)$.

blocks.title: Inversion and Plancherel
blocks.body: If $f$ and $\hat f$ are both absolutely integrable and $f$ is continuous, then $f(x) = \int \hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}\,d\xi$ for every $x$. If $f$ is absolutely integrable and square integrable, then $\int|f|^2 = \int|\hat f|^2$, and the transform extends to an energy-preserving bijection of the square-integrable functions onto themselves.

blocks.title: Why inversion holds, and what it costs
blocks.body:
The proof of inversion copies the proof of Dirichlet's theorem with a better kernel. Insert a Gaussian damping factor: $\int \hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}e^{-\pi\varepsilon\xi^2}\,d\xi$ equals, after Fubini and the Gaussian theorem, the convolution of $f$ with $G_\varepsilon(y) = \varepsilon^{-1/2}e^{-\pi y^2/\varepsilon}$. These Gaussians have total integral 1 and concentrate at 0 as $\varepsilon\to0$, so the convolution tends to $f(x)$ at points of continuity, while the left side tends to $\int\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\xi}\,d\xi$ because $\hat f$ is integrable.

The 'cost' is the uncertainty principle. If $f$ is concentrated near 0 then, by the stretching rule, $\hat f$ is spread out. Quantitatively, for nice $f$,
$$\left(\int x^2|f(x)|^2dx\right)\left(\int \xi^2|\hat f(\xi)|^2d\xi\right) \ge \frac{1}{16\pi^2}\left(\int |f|^2\right)^2.$$
Proof: integrate by parts, $\int|f|^2 = -\int x\,(|f|^2)'\,dx = -2\operatorname{Re}\int x f\,\overline{f'}\,dx$; by [[cauchy-schwarz]] this is at most $2\|xf\|\,\|f'\|$; and $\|f'\| = 2\pi\|\xi\hat f\|$ by Plancherel and the derivative rule. Squaring gives the inequality. Gaussians achieve equality. In quantum mechanics, with $|f|^2$ the position density and $|\hat f|^2$ the momentum density (in suitable units), this is Heisenberg's uncertainty relation.

blocks.title: Two integrals from Plancherel
blocks.body: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}\,dx$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{du}{(1+u^2)^2}$.
blocks.solution:
For the box, $\int|\chi|^2 = 1$, so Plancherel gives $\int \frac{\sin^2\pi\xi}{\pi^2\xi^2}\,d\xi = 1$. Substituting $x = \pi\xi$, $d\xi = dx/\pi$:
$$\frac1\pi\int\frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}\,dx = 1,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}\,dx = \pi.$$
For $e^{-|x|}$, $\int e^{-2|x|}\,dx = 1$, so $\int\frac{4}{(1+4\pi^2\xi^2)^2}\,d\xi = 1$. With $u = 2\pi\xi$, $d\xi = du/(2\pi)$:
$$\frac{4}{2\pi}\int\frac{du}{(1+u^2)^2} = 1,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{du}{(1+u^2)^2} = \frac\pi2.$$
Both can be checked by other methods ([[residues]] for the second), but the Fourier route needs no cleverness once the transforms are known.

blocks.title: Box convolved with itself
blocks.body: Compute $\chi * \chi$ and use the convolution theorem to find the transform of the triangle $\Lambda(x) = \max(1 - |x|, 0)$.
blocks.solution:
$(\chi*\chi)(x) = \int\chi(y)\chi(x-y)\,dy$ is the length of the overlap of $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ and $[x - \tfrac12, x+\tfrac12]$, which is $1 - |x|$ for $|x|\le1$ and 0 otherwise. So $\chi*\chi = \Lambda$, and by the convolution theorem
$$\hat\Lambda(\xi) = \hat\chi(\xi)^2 = \left(\frac{\sin\pi\xi}{\pi\xi}\right)^2.$$
Note how the triangle, which is continuous with corners, has a transform decaying like $1/\xi^2$, one order better than the box. Probabilists will recognise $\Lambda$ as the density of the sum of two independent uniform variables on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$.

blocks.title: The heat equation on a line
blocks.body: Solve $u_t = u_{xx}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$, $t > 0$, with $u(x, 0) = f(x)$.
blocks.solution:
Transform in $x$ for each fixed $t$: $\hat u(\xi,t) = \int u(x,t)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx$. The derivative rule turns $u_{xx}$ into $-4\pi^2\xi^2\hat u$, so for each $\xi$ we get an ordinary differential equation
$$\partial_t\hat u = -4\pi^2\xi^2\,\hat u,\qquad \hat u(\xi,t) = \hat f(\xi)\,e^{-4\pi^2\xi^2 t}.$$
High frequencies are damped fastest, which is why heat flow smooths. By the Gaussian theorem with $a = 1/(4\pi t)$, $e^{-4\pi^2\xi^2t}$ is the transform of
$$H_t(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}e^{-x^2/(4t)},$$
so by the convolution theorem $u(\cdot,t) = H_t * f$. One can check directly that $H_t$ solves $u_t = u_{xx}$ and has total integral 1 for every $t$. More on this in [[heat-equation]].

blocks.body:
- Conventions: with $\hat f(\omega) = \int f e^{-i\omega x}dx$ the inversion formula carries $\frac1{2\pi}$, Plancherel carries $\frac1{2\pi}$, and the derivative rule is multiplication by $i\omega$. Check which convention a formula assumes before using it.
- $\hat f$ need not be integrable even when $f$ is: the box has transform $\frac{\sin\pi\xi}{\pi\xi}$, whose integral converges only conditionally. Inversion then holds in a weaker sense (for instance as a limit of $\int_{-R}^R$), and at the jumps it gives the midpoint value.
- The transform is defined directly by the integral only for absolutely integrable $f$. Functions like $1$, $\sin x$ or $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ need the extended theory (Plancherel's $L^2$ theory or tempered distributions).
- The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma says $\hat f(\xi)\to0$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$, but with no rate in general; decay rates come from smoothness.

The transform grows out of [[fourier-series]], and the two are linked by the Poisson summation formula $\sum_n f(n) = \sum_k\hat f(k)$, discussed in [[fourier-poisson]] and used for theta functions and the functional equation of [[zeta]]. It solves the [[heat-equation]] and [[wave-equation]] on the line and in space, and closely related integral transforms include the [[laplace-transform]] and [[mellin]] transform. In probability, characteristic functions turn sums of independent variables into products, which is the engine behind the central limit theorem in [[limit-theorems]]. The $L^2$ theory is an instance of unitary operators on [[hilbert-spaces]], and on groups other than $\mathbb R$ the same ideas become [[group-representations|representation theory]].

entry.sum: The heat equation $u_t = k\,u_{xx}$ (in higher dimensions $u_t = k\Delta u$) describes how temperature, or any diffusing quantity, evolves: each point moves towards the average of its neighbours. On an interval it is solved by Fourier series, with the $n$-th mode decaying like $e^{-kn^2\pi^2t/L^2}$; on the whole line the solution is the initial data convolved with a Gaussian, the heat kernel, which is also the density of Brownian motion.
key: u_t = k\,u_{xx},\quad u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\, e^{-k n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}
u(x,t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi k t}}\,e^{-(x-y)^2/(4kt)}\,f(y)\,dy \quad\text{on } \mathbb R
\max_{\overline{Q_T}} u = \max_{\text{parabolic boundary}} u \quad\text{(weak maximum principle)}
entry.why: Besides heat conduction it governs diffusion of chemicals, the spread of probability for random walks and Brownian motion, the Black–Scholes model of option prices (after a change of variables), and smoothing filters in image processing. It is the model example of a parabolic PDE, where solutions smooth out instantly and the past cannot be recovered from the present.

links.note: Fourier invented his series to solve the heat equation, and the heat kernel is a standard approximate identity used to sum Fourier series and prove inversion theorems.

The explicit finite-difference scheme for $u_t = ku_{xx}$ is stable only when $k\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le \tfrac12$, the classic example of a stability restriction, which implicit schemes such as Crank–Nicolson avoid.
The heat equation on a Riemannian manifold links the geometry to the spectrum of the Laplacian, and heat-kernel methods give proofs of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem.
